s1.syndrome_frame: asymptomatic cardiac abnormality with murmur in a young adult
salient_findings: systolic murmur in the left upper parasternal region
complete right bundle-branch block on ECG
dilated right atrium and right ventricle on echocardiography
key_facts: 29-year-old primigravida woman
no history of dyspnea, chest pain, palpitation, or lower limb swelling
vital parameters within normal limits
systolic murmur in the left upper parasternal region
normal sinus rhythm with heart rate of 70 beats/min on ECG
complete right bundle-branch block with normal PR interval on ECG
fragmented QRS with a notch on the R wave in inferior leads on ECG
no significant ST-T segment changes on ECG
dilated right atrium and right ventricle on transthoracic echocardiography
large 21-mm defect with left-to-right shunt on transthoracic echocardiography
normal cardiac output on right-sided heart catheterization
step-up in oxygenation from superior vena cava to right atrium
pulmonary vascular resistance: 1.8 Wood units

raw.rationale: The presence of a large 21-mm defect with left-to-right shunt on transthoracic echocardiography, along with a step-up in oxygenation from the superior vena cava to the right atrium, is consistent with an atrial septal defect.

rejected.label: Ventricular Septal Defect
rejected.why: The echocardiogram findings specifically mention a defect with a left-to-right shunt, which is more characteristic of an atrial septal defect than a ventricular septal defect.

rejected.label: Atrioventricular Septal Defect
rejected.why: There is no mention of abnormalities in the atrioventricular valves, which are typically seen in atrioventricular septal defects.

rejected.label: Tricuspid Regurgitation
rejected.why: While tricuspid regurgitation can cause right atrial and ventricular dilation, the primary finding of a large defect with left-to-right shunt points more directly to an atrial septal defect.

rejected.label: Coronary Sinus Atrial Septal Defect
rejected.why: This is a less common type of atrial septal defect, and the provided information does not specifically suggest involvement of the coronary sinus.
